Girondins. A moderate republican faction in the French Revolution who favored decentralized power and constitutional limits on executive authority. The name comes from the Gironde department in southwestern France where many leaders originated, though the faction was actually led from Paris itself. The Girondins advocated for a federal system of regional autonomy rather than centralized power, fearing Paris domination and mob rule by radical sans-culottes. They drew their support from bourgeois merchants, lawyers, and provincial interests, representing the commercially-oriented French regions outside of Paris.

The Girondins controlled the Legislative Assembly from seventeen-ninety-one to seventeen-ninety-two and initially dominated the National Convention starting in September seventeen-ninety-two. They supported the constitutional monarchy under Louis XVI and opposed regicide, believing gradual reform preferable to violent rupture of the established order. Hoping to rally moderates and discredit the radical left, they pushed for war against Austria. Instead, military setbacks strengthened radical influence and made the Girondins appear incompetent and defeatist.

They gradually lost ground to the Montagnards, who appealed to the urban poor with radical ideology and promises of economic intervention, price controls, and revolutionary justice. The crucial difference was that the Montagnards controlled the Paris Commune and the sans-culottes militias, giving them effective power over the Convention despite having fewer formal votes. Between seventeen-ninety-three and seventeen-ninety-four, the Girondins faced systematic destruction. Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety executed twenty-one Girondin leaders in October seventeen-ninety-three and imprisoned dozens more as traitors and counterrevolutionaries. This purge marked the beginning of the Reign of Terror and consolidated Montagnard and Jacobin control over the revolution.

Survivors were posthumously rehabilitated as victims of revolutionary extremism and Robespierre's paranoia, becoming symbols of moderation and principle lost to escalating violence. Their fate demonstrates how moderates could be outpaced by more radical movements and ultimately destroyed.
